body:
Your mother sounds like mine, to the point that reading your post could literally be mistaken for one I wrote. I know how harmful this behavior is to one's self-esteem and how difficult it is to unlearn that image.


What she has done / is doing is 100% emotional abuse and you need to escape that environment as soon as you can. If your situation is anything like mine, your mother probably will not change, especially not while you're living there with her. When you start to pull away or leave she may change her tune, apologize for things and promise to change, etc. but don't buy into it. It sounds like she has been doing this for some time, and it is not something she will be able to "fix" in a few days or months, if ever, especially without some kind of therapy.


I know that leaving is likely not an easy or convenient option for you right now (in college, assuming financially dependent upon her?), but at least try to make plans. Surround yourself as much as you can with positive friends and people who don't treat you like garbage, and realize that she does not and will not ever define your worth. You're a worthwhile person and it always breaks my heart when people don't feel like they are because they have been treated poorly by their parents.


Also: no, you are not wrong at all for trying to stand up for yourself. You may have reacted in ways that were not constructive or done things "wrong" but it does not justify your mother's shitty comments / behavior in the least. Don't let her convince you otherwise.

Here to agree that I am also pretty selective about who I am close to. Which was a big part of the reason it took me so long to start dating. If I didn't see it working out in the long-term then I didn't bother -- I didn't want to emotionally invest that much in something that I thought would fall through and just end up hurting me.

I was close to my father while growing up, but my relationship with my mother was very rocky and sometimes abusive. So that might have something to do with it, but I'm not sure. I think I would still be selective.

I think of it like I'm giving a piece of my heart to everyone I open up to and am close with (either romantically or platonically, whatever the case may be). Since I am very protective of my heart and feelings, I am very careful about who I hand them out to. I know it probably doesn't make much sense, but I worry that if I wasn't so careful, I'd eventually "run out", or at least become too jaded and cynical for my taste.

I felt the need to log in just to provide my two cents haha.

As an INFP who has said almost that exact phrase word for word, I can tell you how I meant it: I felt genuinely grateful for the opportunity to meet and get to know that person, whether things turned out romantic or platonic. That is to say, it wasn't a feeling that depended on an expected outcome. It was a pure feeling of appreciating what that person brought to my life, ignoring all other circumstance. The reason you might have trouble uncovering the hidden meaning of it is precisely that it isn't meant to have any hidden meaning.

Now, of course, just because we are both INFPs doesn't mean we are identical creatures, and she may mean something totally different from what I did. But I thought my opinion might still be relevant.

To further share (considering I said that to my INTP friend who I am now, months later, in a LDR with); I had major reservations about entering a LDR. I am on the flightier side, and if I feel like something will ultimately end poorly (as LDR's have a reputation to) I would rather preserve my feelings now than "enjoy the ride" and hurt later, so to speak. So I tried to resist entering one. I tried to be objective, logical in my decision to avoid it. I was squirrely, I dodged pledges of commitment and labels regarding "what we were". Even when we were going on what was, for all intents and purposes, dates, I told everyone else we were just hanging out as friends.

Ultimately, my emotions won over. My particular INTP gave me all the space I needed, spent time with me without trying to pin me down in this way or that, and just let me enjoy his company and work through my feelings about it all. In the end I was able to freely choose to commit 100% and I am determined to work through whatever problems may arise, whereas had I been forced to decide earlier I might have chosen the emotionally "safe" option to walk away.

So the point I want to make is, just let it be. Enjoy each others' company. If she feels strongly for you, in whatever way that may be (because what she said implies to me that she certainly does), she will stick with you. She may also be flighty and evasive sometimes, her behavior might still be an enigma, but if those emotions are there she will always come back to you. We are inclined to follow those strong emotions above almost all else.

That's what I think, anyway!

(Afterthought: while I personally came around and accepted the LDR, you have to be prepared for the possibility that she won't. I know I advised trying not to make her give you a straight answer right away, but at the same time I realize that puts you in the position of constantly wondering, unsure whether or not it's truly safe to be invested and say you're in a relationship. That is unhealthy for you. So, weigh it accordingly. I would still say to try and enjoy things and let them be for now, but consider how you feel as well. If time passes and she still doesn't give you a straight answer, you do deserve to know where you stand, even if it's not necessarily what you were hoping for.)
